chapters.title: Chapter 1: Anatomy of the Posterior Fossa and Craniocervical Junction
chapters.description: Gross and radiological anatomy of the posterior cranial fossa and upper cervical spine relevant to tonsillar position, CSF flow and potential sites of compression at the foramen magnum.
subtopics: Bony landmarks: occiput, foramen magnum, opisthion, clivus, atlas and axis relationships
Dural reflections, tentorium and foramen magnum dural attachments
Cerebellar anatomy with emphasis on vermis and tonsils
Craniovertebral junction spatial relationships
Normal CSF cisterns and subarachnoid space at the craniocervical junction
Radiologic planes and standard measurements used at C0–C2

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem and Lower Cranial Nerves
chapters.description: Detailed organization of medullary and pontine centres, cranial nerve nuclei (IX–XII) and ascending/descending pathways that mediate autonomic, bulbar and respiratory functions.
subtopics: Medullary respiratory centres: dorsal and ventral respiratory groups, pre-Bötzinger complex
Pontine respiratory modulation: pneumotaxic and apneustic areas
Nuclei of cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII and their functional roles
Nucleus ambiguus, solitary tract nucleus and afferent viscerosensory pathways
Reticular formation and arousal pathways
Descending corticospinal and bulbar motor pathways relevant to voluntary breathing and swallowing

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Physiology of Breathing and Respiratory Control
chapters.description: Integrated physiology of ventilatory control including chemical and neural drivers, voluntary versus automatic breathing, and changes in control during sleep and wakefulness.
subtopics: Central and peripheral chemoreception: CO2 and O2 sensing mechanisms
Mechanoreceptors, pulmonary stretch receptors and reflexes
Automatic (brainstem) versus voluntary (cortical) respiratory pathways
Sleep-state changes in ventilatory control and upper airway tone
Control of breathing during arousal and response to hypoxia/hypercapnia
Physiology of ventilatory drive and perception of dyspnoea

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Pathophysiology of Chiari I Malformation
chapters.description: Mechanisms underlying cerebellar tonsillar descent, posterior fossa volume mismatch, CSF flow disturbance and sequelae such as syringomyelia; distinctions between congenital and acquired forms.
subtopics: Definition and radiographic thresholds for Chiari I malformation
Embryologic and developmental contributors to posterior fossa hypoplasia
Mechanisms of tonsillar herniation and dynamic factors (e.g., trauma, intracranial hypotension)
CSF flow obstruction at the foramen magnum and implications
Pathogenesis of syringomyelia and syringobulbia
Spectrum of anatomical variants versus clinically significant malformations

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Clinical Manifestations of Chiari I
chapters.description: Typical and atypical clinical presentations associated with Chiari I, emphasizing headache phenotypes, cranial nerve dysfunction, gait and cerebellar signs, respiratory and swallowing disorders.
subtopics: Characteristic occipital and Valsalva-associated headaches
Lower cranial nerve symptoms: dysphagia, dysphonia, palatal weakness, tongue atrophy
Cerebellar signs and ataxia
Sleep-related breathing disorders and daytime respiratory symptoms
Pain syndromes including occipital neuralgia and scalp allodynia
Prevalence, natural history and demographic patterns of symptomatic disease

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Sleep-Related Breathing Disorders and Central Sleep Apnoea
chapters.description: Classification, mechanisms and clinical consequences of sleep-disordered breathing, with focus on central apnoea and hypoventilation related to brainstem dysfunction.
subtopics: Distinction between obstructive, central and mixed sleep apnoea
Pathophysiology of central sleep apnoea: ventilatory control instability and failure of automatic drive
Cheyne–Stokes respiration and other central patterns
Impact of central apnoea on gas exchange, sleep architecture and cardiovascular risk
Causes of acquired central apnoea including structural brainstem lesions
Clinical features that differentiate central from obstructive events

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Central Alveolar Hypoventilation Syndromes (Congenital and Acquired)
chapters.description: Overview of syndromes characterized by impaired automatic ventilation, distinguishing congenital genetic forms from acquired causes (trauma, lesions), clinical features and diagnostic criteria.
subtopics: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS): PHOX2B genetics and phenotype
Clinical presentation across lifespan: sleep-predominant hypoventilation, blunted chemosensitivity
Acquired central hypoventilation: mechanisms related to brainstem compression, infarct, demyelination
Diagnostic approach: polysomnography with CO2 monitoring, daytime ABGs and hypercapnic challenge
Prognosis and long-term ventilatory needs
Complications: hypoxaemia without dyspnoea, neurocognitive sequelae

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Neuroimaging of Chiari and Craniocervical Junction Disorders
chapters.description: Principles and interpretation of CT and MRI for evaluating Chiari malformations, CSF flow studies, measurement standards for tonsillar descent, and common pitfalls in imaging reports.
subtopics: MRI sequences critical for Chiari assessment: sagittal T1/T2, FLAIR, cine phase-contrast CSF flow studies
CT imaging roles and limitations at the foramen magnum
Measurement techniques for tonsillar descent and posterior fossa metrics
Identifying crowded foramen magnum and obliteration of subarachnoid spaces
Detection and assessment of syringomyelia and syringobulbia
Common radiologic pitfalls and inter-reader variability

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Principles and Interpretation of Polysomnography and Sleep Studies
chapters.description: Technical aspects, types of sleep studies (type I–III), scoring of respiratory events, and the role of capnography and EEG in diagnosing central hypoventilation.
subtopics: Polysomnography components: EEG, EOG, EMG, airflow, respiratory effort, oximetry, ECG
Differences between type I (full) and limited (type II–III) studies and their diagnostic limitations
Scoring criteria for apnoea, hypopnoea and central vs obstructive events
Apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI) calculation and interpretation
Utility of end-tidal and transcutaneous CO2 monitoring for hypoventilation
Sources of under- and over-estimation (e.g., total recording time vs total sleep time)

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Respiratory Monitoring and Gas Exchange Assessment
chapters.description: Key bedside and laboratory methods to assess oxygenation and ventilation, including pulse oximetry principles, ABG interpretation, and the role of capnography.
subtopics: Pulse oximetry technology, accuracy, artefacts and limitations (motion, poor perfusion, sensor type)
Arterial blood gas (ABG) interpretation: PaO2, PaCO2, pH, alveolar–arterial gradient
End-tidal and transcutaneous CO2 monitoring: principles and clinical uses
Nocturnal oximetry: indications, limitations and interpretation
Relationship between oxygen saturation, PaO2 and hypoventilation
Clinical scenarios where pulse oximetry may miss hypoventilation (normoxia with hypercapnia)

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Pulmonary Function Testing and Respiratory Muscle Assessment
chapters.description: Use and interpretation of spirometry, lung volumes and respiratory muscle strength testing when evaluating neuromuscular and central causes of dyspnoea and hypoventilation.
subtopics: Standard spirometry: FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC ratio and patterns (restrictive vs obstructive)
Maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures (MIP/MEP) as markers of respiratory muscle strength
Indications for full lung volumes and diffusion capacity testing
Interpretation of tests in neuromuscular weakness versus primary pulmonary disease
Role of sniff nasal inspiratory pressure and diaphragmatic function tests
Serial monitoring and thresholds that prompt ventilatory support

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Dysphagia: Neurogenic Mechanisms and Diagnostic Evaluation
chapters.description: Mechanisms of oropharyngeal dysphagia due to neurological disorders, with approaches to evaluation including clinical bedside tests, videofluoroscopic swallow study and fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES).
subtopics: Distinction between oropharyngeal and esophageal dysphagia
Neurogenic dysphagia patterns related to cranial nerve and brainstem lesions
Modified barium swallow (videofluoroscopy): indications and interpretation (aspiration, penetration, pharyngeal transit)
FEES methodology and complementary role to videofluoroscopy
Clinical bedside swallowing assessments and aspiration risk stratification
Management principles: dietary modification, rehabilitative therapy, and indications for enteral feeding

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Differential Diagnosis of Bulbar Dysfunction and Choking
chapters.description: Systematic approach to causes of bulbar symptoms and choking episodes, integrating neurological, otolaryngological and gastroenterological perspectives.
subtopics: Neuromuscular junction disorders: myasthenia gravis evaluation and red flags
Motor neuron diseases (bulbar-onset ALS) and other neurodegenerative causes
Brainstem stroke, demyelinating disease and compressive lesions
Structural lesions of the oropharynx and larynx, and reflux-related laryngopharyngeal disease
Psychogenic and functional causes of choking and cough
Diagnostic algorithms and prioritized testing strategy (ENT, GI, neurology, imaging)

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Neuropathology of Brainstem Compression and Syrinx Formation
chapters.description: Cellular and structural changes that occur with chronic brainstem compression and syringomyelia, and their correlation with clinical deficits.
subtopics: Ischemic and degenerative changes from chronic compression
Pathophysiology of syrinx formation: fluid dynamics, perivascular flow and ependymal injury
Microscopic features: gliosis, demyelination and neuronal loss in brainstem nuclei
Correlation of neuropathology with respiratory, cranial nerve and spinal cord signs
Reversibility of changes after decompression and factors predicting recovery
Animal models and experimental insights into syringogenesis

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Neurosurgical Management of Chiari I Malformation
chapters.description: Indications for surgery, operative techniques for posterior fossa decompression, adjuncts (duraplasty, tonsillar reduction, syrinx drainage) and expected benefits and risks.
subtopics: Clinical and radiographic indications for posterior fossa decompression
Surgical approaches: suboccipital craniectomy, C1 laminectomy, duraplasty options
Role of intraoperative and preoperative CSF flow studies
Techniques for addressing associated syringomyelia (syrinx shunting vs decompression)
Complications: CSF leak, infection, posterior fossa haematoma, cranial nerve injury
Outcomes for headache, neurological deficits and sleep-respiratory abnormalities

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Non‑Surgical and Supportive Management of Central Hypoventilation and Sleep-Related Respiratory Disorders
chapters.description: Medical and supportive interventions for ventilatory failure and sleep-disordered breathing including noninvasive ventilation, CPAP, ventilatory stimulants and rehabilitative strategies.
subtopics: Principles and indications for nocturnal noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP, volume-targeted ventilation)
Use of CPAP for obstructive components and limitations in central hypoventilation
Pharmacologic respiratory stimulants: acetazolamide, theophylline, doxapram—mechanisms and evidence
Nocturnal monitoring, domiciliary oximetry and ventilator follow-up
Acute management of severe hypoxaemia and airway protection
Rehabilitative approaches: respiratory muscle training and multidisciplinary care

chapters.title: Chapter 17: Pharmacology Relevant to Respiratory Drive and Management
chapters.description: Drug effects on ventilatory control, sedatives and opioids risk, and medications used to modulate respiratory drive or treat complications in patients with central hypoventilation and Chiari-related symptoms.
subtopics: Mechanisms by which sedatives, benzodiazepines and opioids depress respiratory drive
Acetazolamide mechanism as a respiratory stimulant and indications
Theophylline and other methylxanthines: pharmacodynamics and adverse effects
Drug interactions and perioperative anesthetic considerations in brainstem-compromised patients
Topical and systemic analgesics used for occipital neuralgia and headache management
Evidence base and limitations for pharmacologic management of central hypoventilation

chapters.title: Chapter 18: Headache Syndromes Associated with Posterior Fossa Pathology and Occipital Neuralgia
chapters.description: Classification and diagnostic approach to headaches that arise from posterior fossa pathology, features of occipital neuralgia and less common scalp pain syndromes.
subtopics: Clinical features distinguishing occipital neuralgia from tension-type and migraine headaches
Diagnostic criteria for occipital neuralgia and relevant peripheral nerve anatomy
Nummular headache, burning vertex syndrome and other localized scalp pain disorders
Role of nerve blocks, peripheral nerve modulation and neurosurgical considerations
Patterns of allodynia and sensory testing of scalp/vertex pain
Approach to headache evaluation when imaging shows posterior fossa abnormalities

chapters.title: Chapter 19: Clinical Significance of Incidental Posterior Fossa Imaging Findings and Variants
chapters.description: Framework for interpreting incidental tonsillar ectopia and crowded foramen magnum on imaging, differentiating innocuous variants from clinically actionable pathology.
subtopics: Prevalence of tonsillar ectopia in the general population and correlation with symptoms
Radiologic features that increase likelihood of symptomatic Chiari (degree of descent, CSF flow obstruction, syrinx)
When to pursue additional testing (cine MRI, sleep studies) for incidental findings
Risk stratification and counseling for asymptomatic patients
Imaging reporting standards and recommended wording to guide clinicians
Follow-up imaging intervals and triggers for referral

chapters.title: Chapter 20: Epidemiology, Risk Factors and Natural History of Chiari Malformations
chapters.description: Population-level data on prevalence, age and sex distributions, genetic and acquired risk factors, and long-term course of Chiari I malformation.
subtopics: Prevalence estimates of Chiari I on imaging versus symptomatic disease rates
Demographic patterns: age at presentation and sex differences
Genetic associations and connective tissue disorders (e.g., Ehlers–Danlos) as risk modifiers
Trauma, intracranial hypotension/hypertension and other acquired precipitants
Natural history of asymptomatic versus symptomatic patients and predictors of progression
Implications for screening family members and counseling

chapters.title: Chapter 21: Multidisciplinary Diagnostic Workflow and Care Pathways
chapters.description: Organization of clinical evaluation for patients presenting with choking, unexplained hypoxaemia or bulbar symptoms, emphasizing coordination between specialties and rational test selection.
subtopics: Roles of primary care, neurology, neurosurgery, ENT, gastroenterology, pulmonology and sleep medicine
Stepwise diagnostic algorithms for dysphagia with normal endoscopy
When to order neuroimaging for bulbar or respiratory presentations
Integration of sleep studies, swallowing studies and pulmonary testing into the workup
Preoperative assessment and optimization prior to posterior fossa surgery
Communication strategies and shared decision-making regarding conservative versus surgical management
